drafting text, providing requested information, coding, searching, implementing).

Short answer: no — don't design the UI first. Run the pipeline manually once, first.

Why the UI-first instinct is a trap here. Designing screens gives you the feeling of clarity, but you'd be designing chat interfaces around a process you haven't actually executed yet. You'd spend a week in Figma and still not know whether your story agent produces something a screenplay agent can use, or whether your quality-check gates catch anything real. Then you rebuild the UI anyway once reality hits.

What actually gives you clarity: do one full episode by hand. Today, in Claude chat, no code, no UI. Blind ideation → story sheet → German check → screenplay sheet → storyboard images → 2× 15-second clips. Whatever it takes. That single run tells you which stages are genuinely valuable, which agent prompts are hard, where the handoff between stages breaks, and where you actually want to intervene as a human. That's your spec — and it's earned, not imagined.

What you're really designing is not screens — it's the artifacts. Your system is essentially four documents flowing through stages:

Universe Bible — 4 characters, visual identity, style locks (static)

Story State — episode number, arcs, open threads (persistent memory = a markdown file, not a fancy system)

Story Sheet — locked output of the ideation phase

Screenplay Sheet — the AI-filmmaking spec, structured per 15-second sequence

Lock those schemas and you've done 80% of the design work. The UI is just a thin wrapper that shows you one artifact at a time with a chat panel beside it.

So the order is: manual episode → write down the four artifact schemas → a rough flow sketch (30 minutes on paper, not a Figma system) → Claude Code with an ugly functional UI → polish visuals last, once the thing produces episodes.

One thing worth flagging: you've described eight-plus agent stages. As a solo builder, that's a lot of surface area for something that has never produced a single finished episode. Build stages 1–3 first (ideation → story → screenplay), keep storyboard and video manual for now, and only automate a stage once you're bored of doing it by hand. Boredom is the correct trigger for automation.
